title: Routes Around Blocked Cells
statement:
A robot stands on the top-left cell of an m × n grid and wants to reach the bottom-right cell. Each move goes one cell right or one cell down. In grid, 1 marks a blocked cell the robot cannot enter and 0 marks a free one.

Return the number of different routes from the start to the goal. If the start or goal is blocked, there are none. Counts can get very large, so return the count modulo 1 000 000 007. (The original guarantees a small answer instead; the modulo lets us test big grids.)

examples.why: The block in the middle leaves only the route along the top then down, and the route down then along the bottom.
A single row: the robot can only move right, and the block cuts it off.
The first column is blocked at row 1, so every cell below it in that column is unreachable too. Filling the first column with 1s would be wrong.

hints: The last move into a cell comes either from above or from the left. How does that relate the route counts?
routes[i][j] = routes[i − 1][j] + routes[i][j − 1] for a free cell, and 0 for a blocked one. What is routes[0][0]?
Fill the table row by row. A single array works: row[j] += row[j − 1] for free cells, row[j] = 0 for blocked ones. Take the modulo on every addition.

explain.intuition:
Every route into cell (i, j) arrives either from the cell above or from the cell to its left, and those two sets of routes never overlap. So the count for a free cell is the sum of the counts above and to the left. A blocked cell has 0 routes through it, and that 0 then flows into everything that would have depended on it.

The first row and column are where people slip. In the obstacle-free version they are all 1s, but here a block in the first column makes every cell below it unreachable. Using the same rule everywhere, with missing neighbours counted as 0, handles that automatically. Since each row only needs the row above, one array of length n is enough.
steps: Create row of length n filled with 0 and set row[0] = 1 if the start is free.
For each row i and column j: if grid[i][j] is 1, set row[j] = 0.
Otherwise, if j > 0, set row[j] = (row[j] + row[j − 1]) mod 1 000 000 007. The old row[j] is the count from above.
pitfalls: Initialising the first row and column to 1 regardless of blocks, as in the third example.
Forgetting a blocked start or goal. Then the answer is 0.
Skipping the modulo until the end. On a 100 × 100 grid the true count overflows 64-bit integers and loses precision in JavaScript numbers.

solutions.title: Try every route recursively
solutions.idea: From each cell, count routes going right plus routes going down. Exponential, because the same cells are recounted many times.

solutions.title: One rolling row
solutions.idea: routes = routes from above + routes from the left; blocked cells reset to 0. Keep only the current row.

followups: The robot may also move diagonally down-right. What changes in the recurrence?
Return the cheapest route when each cell has a cost instead of counting routes.
